Transformers Learn Two Competing Sorting Algorithms,
and Only One Length-Generalizes

Khashayar Gatmiry UC Berkeley & Apple   Nathan W. Henry11footnotemark: 1 UC Berkeley   Chloe H. Su Kempner Institute, Harvard University
Emmanuel Abbe EPFL, Apple   Samy Bengio Apple   Melanie Weber Harvard University   Jonathan A. Kelner MIT
Peter L. Bartlett UC Berkeley & Google DeepMind ††thanks: Equal contribution. Author ordering determined by a coin flip.
Abstract

We show that two-layer transformers trained to near-zero loss on a sorting task converge to one of two mechanistically distinct solution classes depending on their initialization. One solution class consists of solutions that do not use the second attention layer to sort, but also fail to length-generalize. The other, which uses both attention layers, length-generalizes perfectly, despite only being trained to sort sequences of a fixed length. By carefully choosing the weight initialization, we demonstrate that we can steer the model toward learning one solution or the other. We identify input types that are rare at the training length but increasingly common at longer sequence lengths as a source of this disparity in length-generalization, and find that layer-wise specialization of the second class of solutions allows them to handle these rare sequences more accurately. In the second class, we discover a mechanism by which the second layer attention can use the contextual information gathered by the first layer attention to reduce its search space. On the related task of finding the minimum of a sequence, we find a similar two solution-type phenomenon, but with the opposite generalization pattern, where a different form of layer-wise specialization causes the two-layer solution to length-generalize worse than the single-attention solution.

1 Introduction

A recurring hope in mechanistic interpretability is that neural networks trained on well-understood tasks will rediscover familiar algorithms, and that similar mechanisms will recur across independently trained models (Olah et al., 2020; Akyürek et al., 2023). Recent work has complicated this picture by demonstrating settings in which neural networks can implement one of multiple solutions to the same task. For modular addition, Zhong et al. (2023) identified two mechanistically different solutions, termed the “Clock” algorithm and the “Pizza” algorithm (Nanda et al., 2023; Yip et al., 2024, see also), and showed that changes in architectural hyperparameters can determine which solution emerges. Multiple solutions with different generalization behavior out of distribution have since been found in other settings, including in-context learning (Park et al., 2024; Wurgaft et al., 2025), state tracking (Li et al., 2025), and algorithmic tasks such as counting and addition (Zhao et al., 2025). Our paper introduces a new general setting for studying when neural networks converge to one of two qualitatively different solutions. In particular, we study tasks that are possible for a one-layer transformer to implement, and train them with a two-layer transformer.

While common intuition about training dynamics suggests that neural networks have a "simplicity bias" where they tend to converge to simpler solutions, and that simpler solutions generalize better than complex ones (Gatmiry et al., 2024; Du, 2024; Shah et al., 2020), recent work refutes this conventional wisdom (Tsoy and Konstantinov, 2024). We find that under some parameter initializations, these two layer transformers converge to single-stage solutions, where the second attention can be ablated without impacting accuracy, while for other initializations, the transformers converge to a solution that meaningfully uses both attention layers. We find that for the task of minimum-finding, the simpler single-layer solutions generalize better. However, for the task of sorting numbers, we find that the more complex two-layer solutions generalize better, counter to common intuition about simplicity bias. In a third, greedy coin denomination task, we find a larger variation in types of solutions learned, and more mixed results about generalization, but with a correlation between reliance on the 2nd attention layer and length-generalization abilities.

This paper focuses on the task of sorting numbers, where we find the cleanest split in solution types across seeds. We study this task in more detail with mechanistic interpretability, aiming to explain the unintuitive phenomenon of the more complex 2-layer solution length-generalizing better. Sorting a sequence of numbers is a task in 𝐅𝐓𝐂0\mathbf{FTC^{\mathrm{0}}} which can theoretically be performed with just a single layer transformer given a large enough embedding size. In fact, Weiss et al. (2021) show that training a single layer transformer for sorting reaches accuracy close to 1 on the lengths trained on.

We argue for two mechanisms of why length-generalization occurs in the more complex solution. First, the more complex solution learns a form of cross-layer specialization to more accurately sort sequences with numbers close to each other. This is a property of sequences that is rare at the length trained at, but increasingly common at longer evaluation lengths. Second, we show evidence of a hinting mechanism, where the first layer can provide a range of possible next tokens to the second, which may make it easier to select the correct next token out of a candidate set of potential next tokens that grows with larger input lengths. We additionally show how to steer the model toward each solution type by varying the initialization scale across layers.

Organization. Section 2 introduces the task and experimental setup. Section 3 presents the two solution types and describes each at a high level. Section 4 gives a mechanistic analysis of the two-stage solution, identifying two properties that account for its length-generalization advantage. Section 5 investigates what determines which algorithm emerges from training. Section 6 discusses results for algorithms other than sorting, and Section 7 discusses related work.

2 Setup of the Sorting Task

Task. The input to the model is a sequence of KK integers drawn uniformly at random (without replacement) from a vocabulary {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\}, followed by a separator token SEP, after which the model autoregressively outputs them from smallest to largest. Writing the full sequence as x1,…,xK,SEP,xs⁡(1),…,xs⁡(K)x_{1},\dots,x_{K},\text{SEP},x_{s(1)},\dots,x_{s(K)}, where ss sorts the input, the query xs⁡(i)x_{s(i)} must predict xs⁡(i+1)x_{s(i+1)} (and SEP must predict xs⁡(1)x_{s(1)}). We call gi:=xs⁡(i+1)−xs⁡(i)g_{i}:=x_{s(i+1)}-x_{s(i)} the gap at that position. In most experiments, we train on sequences of length K=16K=16 and evaluate length generalization at every KK from 22 to NN, the largest possible sequence.

Architecture. We use a two-layer, causally-masked transformer in the style of nanoGPT, simplified to one attention head per layer to facilitate mechanistic analysis. Crucially, we omit positional encodings (Kazemnejad et al., 2023), which is a necessary condition for length-generalization on algorithmic tasks as any model that encodes absolute position is structurally prevented from generalizing to sequences longer than those seen during training. Furthermore, in our preliminary experiments, we observed that positional embeddings induce more complicated difficult-to-interpret algorithms, with each token attending to itself in a manner that nonetheless becomes mechanistically necessary for accurate model performance. Studies of multiple heads per layer and deeper transformers can be found in Appendix D.

Training. We train online, sampling a new batch of sequences at each iteration. Due to the large space of possible sequences, it is very unlikely to revisit the same input twice, making the distinction between training data and test data on the same sequence lengths not meaningful. We use the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 0.030.03 and a batch size of 40964096, optimizing cross-entropy loss over the output tokens. Models reach 100%100\% training accuracy early in training; we then continue training for a total of 60,00060{,}000 iterations to near-zero loss.

3 Two Sorting Algorithms Emerge from Initialization

Across different weight initializations, with the training data ordering held fixed, we find that trained two-layer transformers achieving perfect sorting accuracy do not all learn the same algorithm. Figure 1 shows that when the second attention layer is removed from the trained model, per-seed accuracy splits into two tight clusters. One cluster retains full sample accuracy, while another cluster of seeds has accuracy tightly clustered around 0. This is in contrast to the first attention layer, which can’t be removed for any seed without dropping the sample accuracy to 0. The fact that the sample accuracy after ablating the second attention is approximately a Bernoulli random variable suggests that there are at least two qualitatively different algorithms that emerge from training, depending on the weight initialization.

We call the algorithm type that does not depend on the second attention a single-stage solution, and the algorithm type that does depend on the second attention a two-stage solution. The distinction between these two solution types has a striking consequence for length-generalization, as two-stage solutions generalize to sequences longer than those seen during training, while single-stage solutions do not (Figure 1). The remainder of this section describes the single-stage solution at a high level. Section 4 then describes how the two-stage solution is different and provides a mechanistic account of why the two-stage solution length-generalizes.

3.1 Single-stage solutions

In single-stage solutions, there is only one attention layer that becomes involved in the computation, and therefore only one query per position to consider. We find that the query at position xs⁡(i)x_{s(i)} attends most strongly to the position holding xs⁡(i+1)x_{s(i+1)} in the unsorted part of the sequence, but also attends partially to positions holding larger values (Figure 2, bottom). The resulting value vector is therefore a linear combination of nearby tokens in sorted order, typically concentrated on the correct one. However, in instances where token attended to most is not the correct next token, the transformer still predicts a correct next token. We hypothesize that the role of the first attention in the single-stage model is to select a set of potential next tokens, which we term the candidate set, consisting of those assigned non-trivial attention probability by the attention. We further hypothesize that the two MLP layers and the unembedding matrix could be thought of as selecting among this candidate set of tokens to produce the correct output.

4 Two-stage solutions and their Mechanistic Analysis

We identify two properties of the two-stage solution that may account for its superior length-generalization. First, the two attention layers specialize across gap sizes between consecutive tokens, where the first layer handles tokens with small gaps to the next largest number, while the second layer has a larger role for tokens where the gap to the next largest token is larger (§4.1). Importantly, sequences with small gap sizes lie in the low-probability tail of the training distribution at small training lengths, so a model can achieve high overall accuracy without handling them reliably. However, as sequence length increases, the gap distribution shifts toward smaller values, making this previously rare statistic increasingly likely. Correctly handling small gaps therefore becomes increasingly important for length-generalization. Second, we provide evidence that the first attention layer can supply the second with contextual information that narrows the search for the correct next token to a smaller interval (§4.2). This windowed monotonicity mechanism may be another factor that allows the second attention layer to maintain an accurate attention distribution even as sequence length grows and tokens become more densely packed.

4.1 Handling Rare Sequences With Specialization Across Layers

While single-stage solutions to the sorting task are measured to have perfect accuracy, we find that they still have adversarial examples. For example, input sequences that are permutations of consecutive integers, with gaps of 11 between sorted input tokens, are unable to be sorted by single-stage models, but can be sorted by two-stage models (see Appendix C for a further study of adversarial examples). As sequence length grows, sequences with smaller gap sizes between tokens become increasingly likely. As we reach an input length equal to the vocabulary size, every gap becomes exactly 1, which we know single stage models are unable to sort, even at short sequence lengths. We hypothesize that the high accuracy of two-stage models on these rare sequences is enabled by a form of layerwise specialization, where tokens of small gaps (whose next largest token is close) are generally handled mostly by the first layer, while predicting large token gaps is handled more by the second layer’s attention. We present three pieces of evidence supporting this layerwise specialization hypothesis in this subsection.

The first attention provides weaker contextual information at large gaps, while the first layer often suffices at small gaps.

As the gap increases, the first attention increasingly attends less to the input sequence, attending more to the separator token, which may act as an attention sink, and also to already sorted inputs, which cannot contain the correct next largest value (Figure 3). This suggests that the first layer’s contribution diminishes as the gap size grows. While for all single-stage seeds, removing the second attention leaves accuracy at 100%100\%, at gap size 11, most two-stage seeds also have accuracy remain at 100%100\% when the second attention is removed (Figure 3). This suggests that any “two-stage” computation matters mainly at medium to large gaps. A minority of seeds, however, do lose accuracy even at gap 11. This diversity suggests that multiple valid solutions exist within the two-stage family, differing in the extent to which the two layers share responsibility at small gaps.

The first layer’s direct path loses causal control at large gaps.

We corroborate this division of labor across gap sizes causally with two interventions. First, we force the first attention to attend to a chosen token only along the pathway that bypasses the second attention, leaving its input to the second attention unchanged. Second, we force the second attention to attend to a chosen token. For each, the hijack success rate is the fraction of interventions that change the prediction to the chosen token. Figure 4 reports the mean hijack success rates of both interventions across six gap sizes, averaged over 23 two-stage seeds (sequence length 3232, vocabulary size 512512). At the smallest gap, there is a very large spread across seeds, similar to the spread seen in Figure 3. The co-success rate at small gaps is approximately 20%, indicating that both pathways can influence the model’s prediction. As the gap grows, the first attention’s direct circuit loses influence, while the second attention hijack success rate remains close to 100%100\% across all gaps, corroborating results found in Figure 3.

4.2 How the first attention can assist the second

While at very small or very large gaps the two-stage model primarily specializes across layers, we believe that at intermediate gaps, common at the training length or medium-long context, both layers play a compositional role in predicting the next token. In this section we describe how we believe the first layer can provide contextual input to the second and how this may assist with length generalization at intermediate lengths.

At average gap sizes, in two-stage models, the second attention markedly attends more reliably to the correct next token than the first, namely ≈99.5%{\approx}99.5\% of the time, versus ≈86%{\approx}86\% for the first (Figure 2). We hypothesize that this difference in accuracy is explained with a hinting mechanism where attention layer 1 supplies attention layer 2 with contextual information that effectively provides an upper bound on the next correct number. This hint originates from the query side, where the first attention gathers contextual information about the current output position and passes it forward through the residual stream, giving the second attention an estimate of where the next sorted value lies. The second attention may then use this signal to adjust the current token’s representation so that its attention is concentrated on the narrow range between the current value and the upper bound provided by the first attention, rather than searching over the entire input sequence.

Isolating the effect of contextual information gathered by the first attention on the second attention.

To better understand how the contextual information gathered by the first attention affects the second attention score, we consider the stylized case where the first attention is concentrated on a single token in the context. We can then analytically characterize the second attention score as a function of four quantities: the query token zz, the key token tt, the first attention target on the query side xx, and the first attention’s target on the key side yy:

s⁡(z,x,t,y)=𝐪​(z,x)⊤​𝐤​(t,y),\displaystyle s(z,x,t,y)\;=\;\mathbf{q}(z,x)^{\top}\mathbf{k}(t,y), (1)

where 𝐪⁡(z,x)=WQ(2)​LN⁡(MLP1⁡(LN⁡(ez+Vx(1))))\mathbf{q}(z,x)=W_{Q}^{(2)}\operatorname{LN}\!\bigl(\operatorname{MLP}_{1}\!\bigl(\operatorname{LN}(e_{z}+V^{(1)}_{x})\bigr)\bigr) and 𝐤⁡(t,y)\mathbf{k}(t,y) is defined analogously. Here Vx(1)V^{(1)}_{x} denotes the first-layer attention’s value vector for token xx (projected through WO(1)W_{O}^{(1)}). The reason we only look into the MLP part of the residual stream after the first layer in Equation 1 is because, as we show in Appendix E, the second attention’s QK scores depend almost exclusively on the first MLP’s output rather than the full residual stream.

Interestingly, as we visualize this score (Appendix E), it is essentially invariant to the key-side target yy of the first attention, but strongly modulated by its query-side target xx, with a high-score band emerging in the interval [z,x][z,x]. That is, the second attention uses contextual information from the first attention exclusively on the query side, consistent with the hinting mechanism described above.

Windowed monotonicity. Given an upper-bound hint xx from the first attention, the second attention does not need to learn a globally correct ranking over the entire vocabulary; it suffices to correctly classify tokens within the window [z,x][z,x]. We hypothesize that this reduced search problem contributes to the second attention’s higher accuracy relative to the first. Figure 5 is consistent with this picture. We intervene on which token the first attention attends to on the query side and measure which key token the second attention attends to most strongly, for a current token of value 250250 (the choice is arbitrary), averaged over 23 seeds. The second attention’s most-attended key usually lies between zz and the first attention’s target, rarely exceeds that target, and increases approximately monotonically with it.

When the first attention’s target is pushed far above the current token, the curve saturates, with the second attention’s most-attended key leveling off at roughly 300300 regardless of how large the target becomes. One interpretation is that the second attention limits how far it follows the upper-bound hint, and stays closer to the local neighborhood of zz when the hint lies far above it (a situation likely very rare during training). Within their respective windows, the second attention’s QK scores also appear smoother than the first attention’s scores (Appendix F), consistent with its narrower search range. The analysis above assumes the first attention is fully concentrated on a single token. When we instead split its weight equally among n∈{2,3,4}n\in\{2,3,4\} tokens spaced δ\delta apart, the band structure persists, and the argmax stays biased toward the smallest token in the attended set rather than the mean (Appendix G), suggesting the mechanism is robust to distributed first-layer attention.

Smaller candidate sets. We measure the number of keys receiving attention weight above 0.040.04, averaged over output positions, as sequence length grows (Figure 5). At the training length, both attention layers of two-stage models attend to about 1.51.5 keys, compared to about 3.63.6 for the first attention of single-stage models. Beyond the training length, the first attention of two-stage models keeps a smaller candidate set than its single-stage counterpart at every length we test (i.e. 3.13.1 versus 8.78.7 keys at 88 times the training length). Since small gaps become more common as sequences grow and the first attention primarily handles small gaps in two-stage models (§4.1), this is the layer we expect to matter most at long lengths. The second attention’s candidate set grows faster, reaching about 66 keys at 1616 times the training length. This is in particular aligned with our observation on length-generalizability of single-stage vs two-stage models in Figure 1.

5 What Determines Which Algorithm Emerges?

5.1 Steering via Initialization Scale

The results so far show that at least two mechanistically distinct solutions coexist in the same loss landscape, with different length-generalization behavior, and the initialization seed determining which one is converged to. If the goal is a model that length-generalizes, one must either train many models and select the generalizing one post hoc, or find a way to bias training toward the desired solution. We show that adjusting the relative initialization scale between the two layers is sufficient to do the latter, enabling the steering of nearly all models towards a pre-specified solution type.

We fix one layer’s weight initialization scale at σ=0.01\sigma=0.01 and increase the other’s to 0.01+|Δ|0.01+|\Delta| (where Δ>0\Delta>0 makes layer 2 larger while Δ<0\Delta<0 makes layer 1 larger), training 100 initialization seeds per condition. At the symmetric baseline, 26% of models are two-stage, while increasing Layer 2’s initialization scale to just σ2=0.013\sigma_{2}=0.013 drives this to 100% (Figure 6). Conversely, increasing Layer 1’s scale to σ1=0.012\sigma_{1}=0.012 drives it to 0% (Figure 6). A plausible explanation is that layers initialized to be larger develop structure first during training as a larger initialization scale makes initial gradients larger. When the first layer is initialized larger, it may learn to solve the task before the second layer ever gets involved, which is consistent with the observation that in single-stage models, the second attention layer almost never attends to the token that the model predicts as the next token, suggesting that it may never have been under gradient pressure to become useful. Models steered this way often retain their solution type’s generalization behavior, with the exception of a small cost when the 2nd layer’s scale is pushed too far, discussed further in Appendix A.2. For the effect of absolute initialization scale rather than relative scale, see Appendix A.1.

5.2 Task difficulty and model capacity bias which solution emerges

Which solution emerges also depends on hyperparameters controlling the task difficulty and the model expressivity. Increasing the vocabulary size NN favors the two-stage solution. In particular, nearly all seeds are single-stage at N=64N=64, while most are two-stage at N=512N=512 (Figure 9), which we hypothesize is because consecutive values become harder for a single attention layer to tell apart (see Appendix B.1). Increasing the embedding dimension EE at fixed N=256N=256 has the opposite effect (Appendix B.2) where the portion of two-stage seeds falls from every seed at E=32E=32 to none at E=80E=80, possibly because wider models can distinguish tokens with a smaller weight norm, which is easier to reach from a small initialization. Together, these suggest that the second layer is recruited when the task is hard relative to the capacity available to solve it (see Appendix B.2 for details). Along with task difficulty and model capacity, we study other factors impacting which solution emerges in the appendix, including the training length, and find a non-monotonic relationship with the solution type (Appendix C).

6 Do these phenomena persist across other algorithms?

While this paper has focused on sorting, where the split between solution types is cleanest, the phenomenon is not specific to sorting. We also study two related tasks that are possible to implement with a single transformer layer, but train them using the same two-layer architecture. Across these tasks, we again find that different initialization seeds lead to solutions that differ in the extent to which they use the second attention layer. We also find that the solution type predicts length-generalization. However, the relationship between using the second layer and length-generalization is not the same across tasks.

The three tasks we study are closely related conceptually. Sorting repeatedly finds the next larger element in the input, while minimum-finding performs only the first step of this procedure, and greedy coin denomination repeatedly finds the largest denomination that does not exceed the current remainder and deducts it from the remainder. Thus, sorting and coin denomination both involve successor or predecessor queries, which only require one layer of a transformer to perform. Despite these similarities, the three tasks produce different distributions of solution types and different patterns of length-generalization.

Minimum-finding.

We train the same two-layer architecture to find the minimum of a length-KK sequence of integers drawn from {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\} with replacement. The input consists of the sequence followed by a separator token, and the model outputs the minimum value. We train at K=16K=16 with N=4096N=4096 and evaluate at longer sequence lengths.

One important distinction between the sorting task and the minimum-finding task is that for the minimum-finding task, we sample input sequences with replacement. Sorting with duplicates cannot be performed by a single attention layer without positional encodings, since the model must keep track of how many copies of each value to output. Minimum-finding, in contrast, remains possible with one layer because the output does not depend on a value’s multiplicity. Minimum-finding therefore lets us compare single-stage and two-stage solutions on inputs with duplicates.

Greedy coin denomination.

We also study the task of greedy coin denomination. The input is a set of distinct denominations, followed by a separator token and a target value. The model must output the sequence of remainders produced by repeatedly subtracting the largest denomination that does not exceed the current remainder. We train on denomination sets of size K=8K=8 and evaluate on larger sets. This task is closely related to sorting because at each output step, the model must find the largest available denomination below the current remainder. This is a predecessor query, whereas sorting requires a successor query. We study the greedy algorithm rather than the optimal change-making algorithm since it is an easier task that can be done with a single-layer transformer, although it is not optimal for every set of denominations.

Choice of vocabulary and initialization scale.

For both tasks, we choose the vocabulary size so that it is small enough for a single-stage solution to be learnable, but large enough that the model sometimes learns to use the second layer. Since minimum-finding is easier than sorting, we use a larger vocabulary for minimum-finding (N=4096N=4096, compared with N=256N=256 for sorting) before two-stage solutions appear at appreciable rates. We then choose a symmetric initialization scale at which both solution types occur at similar rates. For minimum-finding, we use σ=0.006\sigma=0.006, selected from a scan over σ∈[0.005,0.01]\sigma\in[0.005,0.01]; for coin denomination, we use σ=0.1\sigma=0.1.

6.1 Different tasks produce different solution types

Figure 1 shows the results for all three tasks. As with sorting, ablating the second attention layer separates models according to how much they use the second layer. Some models are almost completely unaffected by the ablation, indicating that they have learned a single-stage solution. Other models fail after the ablation, indicating that they use both attention layers. For sorting, the two-stage models length-generalize better than the single-stage models. Greedy coin denomination shows the same overall pattern, where models that rely more on the second attention layer tend to generalize better, although the solutions form a more continuous range than they do for sorting. Minimum-finding shows the opposite pattern, where the single-stage models generalize better than the two-stage models. Whether the two-stage solution aids length-generalization is therefore a property of the task.

6.2 Competing failure modes in minimum-finding

The minimum-finding result can be understood by comparing the adversarial examples of the two solution types. Both solution types achieve high accuracy at the training length, but they fail on different types of inputs. In particular, two-stage models degrade when many input values are close to the minimum. These inputs are rare at the training length, but become increasingly common as the sequence length grows. Single-stage models are more robust to these inputs, but are less robust than two-stage models to inputs involving duplicate numbers.

One hypothesis is that duplicates are difficult because they require more precise attention scores. Suppose the minimum has pre-softmax score a1a_{1}, while each of nn copies of the second-smallest value has score a2a_{2}. To place more total attention on the minimum, the model needs ea1>n​ea2e^{a_{1}}>ne^{a_{2}}, or equivalently a1−a2>log⁡na_{1}-a_{2}>\log n. Thus, the required score margin grows with the number of copies of a competing value. The additional layer in the two-stage models may help make these distinctions. This would explain why they handle some duplicate-related inputs better, but fail on crowded near-minimum inputs.

These results suggest that length-generalization depends on how a solution’s failure modes interact with the shift in input distribution. In sorting, the two-stage solution handles small-gap inputs, which become more common at longer lengths. In minimum-finding, the two-stage solution instead appears to fail on inputs with many values close to the minimum, which are the ones that become more common, while performing better on some inputs involving duplicates. More generally, additional expressivity may help a model handle some input types that are rare at the training length, and whether this improves length-generalization depends on whether those input types become important at longer lengths. Studying the minimum-finding and coin denomination solutions in more depth, and building a more general understanding of how and when this occurs, is an interesting direction we leave for future work.

7 Related Work

7.1 Transformer sorting and length-generalization

Prior work studies sorting as a canonical algorithmic task for transformers and situates it within the broader problem of length-generalization (Anil et al., 2022). It has been shown that transformers can be constructed to sort (Lindner et al., 2023; Awasthi and Gupta, 2023), and that whether trained ones length-generalize depends strongly on properties of the set-up, such as positional encodings (Kazemnejad et al., 2023). Yan et al. (2020) also found that transformers trained to sort have difficulty distinguishing numerically close inputs, and separately that their attention loses sharpness beyond the training length. We connect the two observations by noting that that close values are rare at the training length but common at longer ones, and show how the two solution types handle them differently through layer-wise specialization. More broadly, Zhou et al. (2023) propose the RASP-Generalization Conjecture, which predicts that transformers tend to length-generalize when a task admits a short RASP-L program that works for all input lengths, which includes sorting. Our results suggest a complementary complication, that even when such solutions exist, training need not reliably recover the same one (Zhou et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025, cf. the seed sensitivity reported by), and different learned algorithms can have different length-generalization behavior. While these works help answer the question of whether transformers can length-generalize, our work focuses on the analysis of what models learn in practice, studying internal mechanisms of learned algorithms, what drives the model to converge to different solutions, and how to control this process.

7.2 Mechanistic analysis and multiple learned solutions

Huang et al. (2026) show that length-generalizing transformers often admit compact, interpretable RASP subprograms that suffice for their behavior, providing direct evidence that trained models can internally implement simple algorithmic programs. Urdshals and Urdshals (2025) study how internal structure develops in a list-sorting transformer during training, identifying emergent head specializations shaped by the data, but don’t study the behavior in more complex, multiple layer models, or study length-generalization. Awasthi and Gupta (2023) probe a two-layer sorting transformer and find successor-like computation after the second attention layer that the final MLP then cleans up, resembling our two-stage solution. Li and McClelland (2022) also train two-layer transformers on a multi-feature sorting task that their single-layer model fails to learn, and study how the learned solutions decompose the task across layers.

A separate line of work asks whether models trained on the same task converge to a single mechanism or to multiple distinct solutions. Zhong et al. (2023) argue that even simple tasks can admit qualitatively different mechanistic solutions, while recent follow-up work argues that some of these apparent differences may be different weight/neuron instantiations of the same underlying algorithm, which is reflected in the underlying geometry (Moisescu-Pareja et al., 2025). In in-context learning, models shift between memorizing and generalizing strategies depending on data diversity and training time (Park et al., 2024; Wurgaft et al., 2025). Multiple learned mechanisms have also been reported for state tracking (Li et al., 2025), and for algorithmic tasks such as counting and addition, where outcomes vary substantially across random seeds (Zhao et al., 2025).

7.3 Initialization scale and attention dispersion

Zhang et al. (2025) show that the global initialization scale determines whether transformers learn compositional or memorizing solutions. However, they focus on a different setting, and we instead steer via the relative scale of two layers, where both of our solutions are exact in distribution. Veličković et al. (2025) show that softmax attention necessarily disperses as the number of keys grows; the two-stage solution’s hint mechanism can be seen as one way a model counteracts this, by shrinking the candidate set (§4).

8 Conclusion

In this paper, we studied what transformers do with capacity they do not need. Every task we considered can be solved by one attention layer, yet a two-layer model sometimes leaves the second layer unused and sometimes recruits it, depending on the random initialization, and length generalization abilities vary in these different cases. Whether a model uses capacity it does not need is an outcome of training that we find can be steered, here by the relative initialization scale of the layers. Because the more complex solution generalizes better for some tasks and worse for others, contrary to common intuition, it is important to take away that simplicity alone does not predict out-of-distribution behavior. Importantly, we unravel the mechanism by which the second attention uses the contextual information gathered by the first attention to provide a more accurate prediction. An interesting open question is whether we can characterize such cooperative structures between layers in deeper sorting models. Other open questions include whether the eventual solution can be predicted reliably early in training, and whether the same seed-dependent selection occurs in larger models trained on natural data.

Author Contributions

KG started the project performing an in-depth mechanistic analysis of the single-stage sorting solution. NH found that there was more than one solution type transformers learned depending on the random seed, and KG and NH worked to characterize and analyze the solution types, with specific contributions outlined below. NH identified the relevance of token gap size, finding adversarial examples in single-stage models and discovering the layer-wise specialization to different gap sizes in two-stage models (Figures 3, 3). NH led the study of what factors affect which solution type emerges, discovering how one can control which model emerges based on the initialization (Figure 6) and analyzing other factors impacting which solution emerges (Appendix A, B.1, and C). KG later contributed to this exploration studying the impact of embedding sizes in Appendix B.2. NH also discovered a broader set of tasks exhibiting single- and two-stage solutions (Figure 1 and Section 6) and studied how results extend to settings with models deeper than 2 layers and models with more than one head (Appendix D).

KG did extensive experiments to understand how robust single and two-stage models are with respect to manipulating their attention scores. These culminated in KG designing the hijacking experiments (Figure 4), which causally characterized how direct first-layer circuits and first-to-second-layer hinting circuits contribute separately and jointly to the output, extending and corroborating NH’s observations of these distinct computational routes. KG also characterized how the contextual information gathered by the first-layer attention is used by the second-layer attention in two-stage models (Appendix G, F, Section 4.2). KG discovered a mechanism by which the first layer can provide hints to the second to search in a smaller space, termed the windowed monotonicity mechanism (Figure 5), providing an explanation for the second layer having more accurate attention probabilities than the first in some settings, initially identified by NH. KG also analyzed the size of the set of keys with nontrivial attention probability and its connection to the length generalization across different solution types (Figure 5). KG also characterized which circuits actively contribute to the residual stream in a typical two-stage model checkpoint (Appendix E, H).

CS contributed to the length-generalization experiments and played a substantial role in the early experimental design, framing, and presentation of the paper. All authors contributed to the writing of the manuscript.

Appendix A The Impact of Initialization Scale

A.1 The impact of changing initialization scale symmetrically

Section 5 showed that the relative initialization scale between layers steers which solution type emerges. Here we examine the effect of absolute initialization scale, where both layers are initialized at the same standard deviation σ\sigma. Figure 7 suggests that there may be three different regimes as σ\sigma varies. For very small initialization scales, the outcome is approximately unbiased, where each solution type emerges roughly 50% of the time, as if the initialization carries negligible information about which algorithm will be favored. For very large initialization scales, nearly all seeds converge to the single-stage (non-length-generalizing) solution. For intermediate initialization scales, we find that the behavior is less predictable, where some values of σ\sigma favor two-stage solutions while others consistently favor single-stage solutions.

A.2 Length Generalization of Asymmetrically Steered Models

The bottom panel of Figure 6 shows length generalization curves for all models in each condition, colored by solution type. At a qualitative level, two-stage models (blue) generalize, while single-stage models (red) do not, regardless of the difference in initial scale Δ\Delta. However, we find a surprising sensitivity to relative initialization scale in that once the initialization of the second layer initialization is too strong, the model occasionally exhibits less cross-layer specialization (see Figure 8), and has poorer length-generalization.

Appendix B The impact of vocabulary size and embedding dimension

B.1 Varying vocabulary size

Section 5.2 reports that larger vocabularies favor the two-stage solution while wider models favor the single-stage one. Figure 9 varies the vocabulary size NN with all other hyperparameters fixed, using 100 seeds per vocabulary size. One potential interpretation of this phenomenon is that with larger vocabularies comes a harder discrimination problem, where with more possible token values, consecutive elements of the sorted output would be closer in embedding space, potentially making it more difficult for a single attention layer to reliably distinguish between them. Under this pressure, the network may be incentivized to use a more compositional solution from the start using the second layer.

B.2 Varying embedding dimension

One would expect capacity to act in the opposite direction as task difficulty. With a higher embedding dimension, the token representations have more mutually near-orthogonal directions available, so the query-key inner products that order the candidate tokens can be realized at a smaller embedding norm. Since the weights begin at a small initialization scale, a solution expressible at smaller norm should be easier for the optimizer to reach, and increasing the embedding dimension should therefore favor the single-stage solution. We vary the embedding dimension at a fixed vocabulary size (256) and sequence length (1616), and estimate each width from a common sample of 7070 seeds that learned the task. Figure 10 confirms the prediction, showing that the two-stage share falls from every trained seed at embedding size 3232 to none at 8080.

Appendix C Training across varying input lengths

Our explanation of the two-stage model’s length generalization rests on the gap distribution. When KK values are drawn from a vocabulary of size NN, the mean gap between consecutive sorted values is (N+1)/(K+1)(N+1)/(K+1), so small gaps are rare at short training lengths and common at long ones. The training length therefore sets how often a model sees the inputs that the first attention layer of two-stage models specializes in (§4.1). To test this, we vary the training length while holding the vocabulary fixed at N=256N=256. We train 5050 seeds at each training length K∈{4,…,16,24,32,48,64}K\in\{4,\dots,16,24,32,48,64\} and classify each seed that learns the task based on reliance on the 2nd attention layer, as in the main text. We note that, interestingly, the share of two-stage models changes with training length non-monotonically (Figure 11).

Which two-stage models length-generalize?

At K≥16K\geq 16, every two-stage model generalizes essentially perfectly to the longest evaluation length. At shorter training lengths, however, generalization varies from one two-stage model to another and no seeds lead to perfectly length-generalizing models. We hypothesize this is because the frequency of tokens that have small gaps is much smaller when the training length is 4, so less expressivity is allocated to this. One property from the main text that predicts this variation is the amount of attention that the first layer places on the input sequence when the gap is 11 (Figure 12). Models whose first layer attends more to the input at small gaps (a property associated with exhibiting more gap-based specialization across layers) generalize further. In particular, the correlation with token accuracy at evaluation length 256256 is r=+0.77r=+0.77 at K=4K=4, where we see the most variation in generalization abilities across seeds. We also find that models with smaller candidate sets generalize further (Figure 13), achieving a similarly high anti-correlation between length-generalization abilities and candidate set size. Both results provide additional evidence that supports the two mechanisms of Section 4.1 and Section 4.2.

Adversarial inputs across training lengths.

As noted in the main text, we found that inputs consisting of permutations of consecutive sequences of numbers serve as adversarial examples to single-stage solutions, but are handled correctly by two-stage solutions. Here we inspect the extent to which models trained on different sequence lengths are exposed to similar kinds of adversarial examples. In particular, we plot the prevalence of small-gap adversarial examples and large-gap adversarial examples for single-stage and two-stage models across training lengths (Figures 14, 15).

Small-gap adversarial examples (Figure 14). We first consider inputs consisting of permutations of runs of nn consecutive integers, where the remaining K−nK-n values are sampled randomly outside the span of the run. We score accuracy only on the n−1n-1 positions inside the run. For K≥12K\geq 12, two-stage models have an accuracy remaining at 11 for every run length. This includes a fully consecutive sequence at K=32K=32 (whose expected frequency in training is 10−3910^{-39}), where single-stage models score 0.890.89. Single-stage models become more robust to smaller gaps as KK grows and small gaps become more common in training, and at K=64K=64 even single-stage models score 1.001.00 on a fully consecutive sequence. However, for very large training lengths, while you see small gaps more often, large gaps become increasingly uncommon.

Large-gap adversarial examples (Figure 15). Each large-gap adversarial example contains a single adjacent pair v,v+gv,v+g with the interval between them left empty, and we score accuracy on the one prediction that must jump from vv to v+gv+g. Every model handles gaps up to some size and then fails abruptly. The maximum gap that can be predicted accurately shrinks as the training length grows, following the mean gap seen in training, and two-stage models typically handle larger gaps than single-stage models trained at the same length. We believe that this is further attributed to gap-wise specialization across layers. Together, these two families of adversarial examples provide additional evidence suggesting that the gap distribution that the model is trained on impact what inputs a model can handle. Longer training lengths make models robust to small gaps but vulnerable to large ones, and shorter training lengths make models more accurate at large gaps but worse with small ones, leading to the worse length-generalization we see for models trained at small lengths.

Appendix D Sorting in Deeper Transformers and Multi-headed Transformers

Given the existence of single-stage solutions to sorting, we know that a single attention layer with a single head is sufficient to sort. As a result, our main experiments training two-layer models are partially motivated by training a model with one more layer than it needs, where we find that whether it uses the second layer depends on the seed. Here, we ask whether the same holds when the model has more spare capacity, either as additional layers beyond 2 (Appendix D.1) or as additional heads within one layer (Appendix D.2).

D.1 Four-layer transformers

We also train deeper transformers on the sorting task. While two-layer transformers learned one of two solution types (the single-stage or two-stage solution), we find that four-layer transformers learn one of four solution types, where in each type, different attention layers are removable.

Setup.

We use the same architecture as in Section 2 (one head per layer, embedding dimension 6464, and no positional embeddings), with four transformer layers instead of two. They are trained to sort sequences of length 16 from a vocabulary of size 128, using AdamW with a learning rate of 0.020.02 and a batch size of 40964096, and a cosine schedule with 200200 warm-up steps for 2000020000 iterations. We compare two initialization conditions on the same 5050 seeds, one with the same initialization scale for every layer (0.010.01) and one with a lower scale for every layer after the first (σ1=0.01\sigma_{1}=0.01 and σ2=σ3=σ4=0.005\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{3}=\sigma_{4}=0.005).

Solution types.

To find which layers a model needs, we zero attention layers of trained models and re-evaluate. A series of layers counts as removable if the full sequence accuracy stays at or above 0.9990.999. However, the number of removable layers is very robust to this threshold number. We define a model’s solution type by the number of layers it cannot do without, including one (only the first layer is needed), two (only the first two), three (only the first three), and four (every layer is needed). We find that the necessary layers always form such a contiguous sequence of necessary layers (i.e. only the fourth layer can be removed if one is only removing one attention layer).

Initialization steers how many layers are used.

Figure 16 displays the distribution of solution types for 4-layer transformers trained on the sorting task. Under equal scales, some seeds require four, three, and two layers to sort, and none of the seeds reduce to just a single layer, even though one would be sufficient. Lowering the scale of layers 2 through 4, however, produces 14 models that run on the first layer alone. This mirrors the two-layer setting (Section 5), where making the first layer relatively larger at initialization favors the single-stage solution.

Length generalization still requires at least two layers.

Like with the two-layer set-up, in the four-layer set-up we call a model single-stage when it works when all attention layers but the first are ablated. Mimicking the two-layer case, single-stage models also fail to length-generalize (Figure 17), while any seed using more than one layer succeeds in length generalization (like the two-stage solutions in the two-layer set-up).

We do not attempt to characterize three- and four-layer solutions mechanistically. A cursory exploration led us to find that the mechanisms identified for two layers do not generalize neatly to more layers. In particular, there does not appear to be a clean layer-wise specialization of tokens, and there does not appear to be a more general divide and conquer strategy that appears as solutions get deeper (i.e. candidate sets do not get iteratively smaller).

D.2 Multiple heads per layer

We next give the model spare capacity within a layer instead of adding additional layers. While with two layers, whether the second layer is used depends on the seed, we find that when we extend to multiple heads, all seeds require all heads for performance and the variation across seeds exists only for whether or not the second layer is used rather than whether one or multiple heads are used.

Setup.

We train models with vocabulary size 256 and a training length of 16 using the same training recipe of Section 2, varying both the number of layers and the number of heads per layer HH. The HH heads of a layer split into heads of dimension dmodel/Hd_{\text{model}}/H. We remove a head by zeroing its output before the layer’s output projection. Heads within a layer are interchangeable, so for each model we remove the head whose removal results in the lowest loss in accuracy.

Whether a second layer is used varies by seed, while a second head is always used across seeds.

Figure 18 compares the two kinds of spare capacity (spare layers and spare heads). The second layer is removable without loss for some seeds in both single-head models and two-head models, depending on the seed. In one-layer models with two heads, with dmodel=128d_{\text{model}}=128, where either head would be large enough on its own, ablating a head causes all 2020 models to lose most of their accuracy. The same holds for heads of both layers in the two-head, two-layer models at dmodel=48d_{\text{model}}=48 (excluding the 55 single-stage seeds, where one would be able to ablate any of the second layer’s heads since the entire attention layer is removable). Thus, we find that when an attention layer is used by the model, all of its heads are used. We note that this holds for up to three heads per layer. With 44 or 88 heads per layer, we note that removable heads in a used second layer become more common.

A second head prevents the length-generalization failure.

We find that the length-generalization failure of single-stage solutions in the main text is specific to one head per layer (Figure 19). With one head, single-stage models fail at long lengths while two-stage models do not (Figure 19 (a)). With two heads, every model is single-stage, yet all of them length-generalize (Figure 19 (b)). The same holds for one-layer models, which have no second stage at all (Figure 19 (c)). We find that this is not particular to one width, as models with two heads and two layers length-generalize at every width and initialization scale that we trained, regardless of their solution type.

Appendix E Second Attention QK Scores Depend Predominantly on MLP1 Output

In the main text (§4.2) we write the second attention score as a function s⁡(z,x,t,y)s(z,x,t,y) of only four quantities: the query token, the key token, and the first attention’s target on each side. This simplification is justified because, in the majority of two-stage checkpoints, the second-layer attention scores are predominantly determined by the first-layer MLP output alone. In particular, replacing the second attention’s input with the first MLP’s output causes negligible changes in both the attention distribution and full-model accuracy. We verify this across a grid of sequence lengths K∈{16,32}K\in\{16,32\} and vocabulary sizes N∈{128,256,512,1024}N\in\{128,256,512,1024\} with 5 random seeds each (40 checkpoints total), of which 15 are classified as two-stage models (i.e., full-sequence accuracy drops to near zero when the second attention is ablated). We exclude two outlier checkpoints at vocabulary size 10241024 discussed below, leaving 13 for detailed analysis. For each checkpoint we evaluate on 5,000 randomly sampled sequences, measuring over all output positions. We perform two complementary measurements.

Distributional similarity.

We compare the second attention’s probability distribution computed from the full residual stream (𝐞+𝐚1+𝐦1\mathbf{e}+\mathbf{a}_{1}+\mathbf{m}_{1}) against the distribution computed from only the MLP1 output (𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{1}), with embeddings and the first attention’s output zeroed out. We report the per-position ℓ1\ell_{1} distance d=∑j|pnormal​(j)−pmlp1-only​(j)|d=\sum_{j}|p_{\text{normal}}(j)-p_{\text{mlp1-only}}(j)|, which ranges from 00 (identical) to 22 (disjoint). All 13 checkpoints exhibit mean ℓ1\ell_{1} distances below 0.030.03, with all five seeds at sequence length 3232 and vocabulary size 512512 yielding d≈0.005d\approx 0.005 (Figure 21).

Full-model accuracy.

As a functional test, we also measure the model’s full-sequence sorting accuracy when the second attention’s input is restricted to MLP1 output only (while all other components, including MLP2 and the final readout, receive the normal residual stream augmented with this modified second attention output). Figure 22 shows that the accuracy drop is zero or negligible across all 13 checkpoints (maximum drop 0.05%0.05\%), confirming that the embedding and first attention components of the residual stream carry no information that the second attention functionally relies on.

Outliers.

Two of the 15 two-stage checkpoints at vocabulary size 10241024 (sequence length 1616, seed 3, d=0.133d=0.133; sequence length 3232, seed 5, d=0.299d=0.299) deviate from this pattern, showing that the second attention can also learn to exploit other residual stream components. Since other seeds at vocabulary size 10241024 do not exhibit this behavior, it appears to be seed-dependent rather than determined by vocabulary size. We note that the MLP1-only dependence is a common empirical feature of two-stage models in our setting, not a necessary architectural property.

Appendix F Smoothness Advantage of the Second Attention over the First

Figure 23 overlays the first attention’s QK score (for query token 250250 vs. all keys) with the second attention’s QK scores at three query-side targets. The first attention’s curve is noisy across the full vocabulary range, reflecting the difficulty of maintaining monotonicity over 512512 tokens. The second attention’s curves, by contrast, are visibly smoother in their respective windows—the narrower the window, the easier it is for the learned embeddings to maintain a clean monotonic profile.

Appendix G How second attention uses the hint from the first attention when its score is nontrivial on multiple tokens

The windowed monotonicity analysis in §4.2 assumes the first attention places its full weight on a single token xx. In practice, the first attention distributes weight over a small candidate set (typically 2–3 tokens above an attention threshold of 0.040.04). To test the robustness of our hypothesis in section 4.2 on how second attention uses the contextual information from the first attention, instead of assuming the first attention is only concentrated on one token, we generalize it by studying the case when the first attention is concentrated on a set of nn equidistant numbers {xm​i​n,xm​i​n+δ,…,xm​i​n+(n−1)​δ}\{x_{min},x_{min}+\delta,\dots,x_{min}+(n-1)\delta\} spaced by δ\delta. Consistent with our notation in section 4.2, the query embedding of the second-layer attention is now given by

𝐪⁡(z,x,n,δ)=WQ(2)​LN⁡(MLP1⁡(LN⁡(ez+Vs​p​l​i​t​(x,n,δ)))),\displaystyle\mathbf{q}(z,x,n,\delta)=W_{Q}^{(2)}\operatorname{LN}\!\bigl(\operatorname{MLP}_{1}\!\bigl(\operatorname{LN}(e_{z}+V_{split}(x,n,\delta))\bigr)\bigr),

where

Vsplit​(x,n,δ)=1n​∑i=0n−1Vx+i​δ(1),V_{\text{split}}(x,n,\delta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}V^{(1)}_{x+i\delta},

and x=xminx=x_{\min} denotes the smallest token in the set.

Similarly, the second attention score s⁡(z,x,t,y,n,δ)s(z,x,t,y,n,\delta), which now also depends on n,δn,\delta is given by

s⁡(z,x,t,y,n,δ)=𝐪​(z,x,n,δ)⊤​𝐤​(t,y,n,δ).\displaystyle s(z,x,t,y,n,\delta)\;=\;\mathbf{q}(z,x,n,\delta)^{\top}\mathbf{k}(t,y,n,\delta). (2)

We evaluate n∈{2,3,4}n\in\{2,3,4\} and δ∈{1,5,20}\delta\in\{1,5,20\} for the same query token z=250z=250 and the key-side configuration used in the main text. As we mentioned before, the second attention score depends almost entirely on yy, namely the contextual information gathered by attention one on the key side. Since in our experiments we also fix the query token zz, we abbreviate s⁡(z,x,t,y,n,δ)s(z,x,t,y,n,\delta) by s⁡(x,t,n,δ)s(x,t,n,\delta) or s⁡(xm​i​n,t,n,δ)s(x_{min},t,n,\delta).

Heatmaps.

Figure 24 compares the second attention’s QK score heatmap (query-side target on the yy-axis, key token on the xx-axis) for n=1n=1 (single focus) through n=4n=4 (four-way split, δ=5\delta=5). The band structure—elevated scores in a window above the diagonal—is preserved in all cases. As the number of attended tokens increases, the heatmap becomes slightly smoother but the overall geometry is unchanged.

Score Slices.

Figure 25 shows the second attention’s QK score slices for the two-token split (n=2n=2) at δ∈{1,5,20}\delta\in\{1,5,20\}, with the same query token (z=250z=250) and query-side targets (xmin∈{260,270,280,290,300}x_{\min}\in\{260,270,280,290,300\}) as in the main text. Figures 26–27 extend this to n=3n=3 and n=4n=4. In every configuration, the band structure and monotonicity are preserved. As δ\delta increases, the argmax shifts slightly toward larger key values, consistent with the larger tokens in the split exerting a secondary upward pull on t∗t^{*}. The effect remains modest: even at n=4n=4, δ=20\delta=20 (spanning a range of 60 tokens), the windowed monotonicity structure is clearly preserved.

Argmax Bias Toward xminx_{\min}

When the first attention splits its weight across nn tokens {xmin,xmin+δ,…,xmin+(n−1)​δ}\{x_{\min},x_{\min}+\delta,\ldots,x_{\min}+(n-1)\delta\}, the effective query-side signal is a blend of their value vectors. A natural question is whether the argmax of the second attention’s QK score, t∗=arg⁡maxt⁡s⁡(xm​i​n,t,n,δ)t^{*}=\arg\max_{t}s(x_{min},t,n,\delta), tracks the minimum token xminx_{\min}, the mean xmeanx_{\mathrm{mean}}, or the maximum xmaxx_{\max} of the attended set.

Figure 28 provides three complementary views. The left panel fixes δ=5\delta=5 and varies n∈{1,2,3,4}n\in\{1,2,3,4\}: all curves track close to xminx_{\min} and remain well below the t∗=xmint^{*}=x_{\min} diagonal (reflecting the argmax saturation from the main text), with only minor differences between nn values. The middle panel fixes n=3n=3 and varies δ∈{1,5,10,20}\delta\in\{1,5,10,20\}: the argmax is largely insensitive to δ\delta, confirming that the additional higher-valued tokens in the split exert minimal upward pull on t∗t^{*}. This shows that the argmax of the second attention score varies mostly as a function of xm​i​nx_{min} and does not strongly depend on nn or δ\delta.

The right panel aggregates all (n,δ,xmin)(n,\delta,x_{\min}) configurations in a scatter of (t∗−xmin)(t^{*}-x_{\min}) versus (t∗−xmean)(t^{*}-x_{\mathrm{mean}}). The mean offsets (diamonds) show that |t∗−xmin||t^{*}-x_{\min}| is consistently much smaller than |t∗−xmean||t^{*}-x_{\mathrm{mean}}| for n>1n>1, indicating that the argmax is biased toward the smallest token in the attended set rather than its average.

This xminx_{\min} bias is functionally advantageous for sorting. Since the first attention identifies the next-smallest candidates above the current position’s value zz, the key token that the second attention should attend to is determined primarily by the smallest candidate, not by an average over all candidates. By anchoring t∗t^{*} near xminx_{\min}, the second attention’s QK mechanism effectively ignores the distractors that the first attention also partially attends to, preserving the conservative “look just above zz” strategy described in the main text.

Appendix H Residual Stream Cleanup: Redundant Direct Paths

The residual stream after both layers contains five additive components: 𝐞\mathbf{e} (token embedding), 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} (first attention output), 𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{1} (MLP1 output), 𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{2} (second attention output), and 𝐦2\mathbf{m}_{2} (MLP2 output). We ask whether each component’s direct additive contribution to the residual is necessary for the correct prediction, or whether its information is already subsumed by downstream components that consumed it as input.

Claim 1: 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} is redundant after feeding MLP1.

We remove 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} from the residual stream immediately after it has served as input to MLP1 (which sees LN2​(𝐞+𝐚1)\mathrm{LN}_{2}(\mathbf{e}+\mathbf{a}_{1})). The modified residual entering block 2 is 𝐞+𝐦1\mathbf{e}+\mathbf{m}_{1} instead of 𝐞+𝐚1+𝐦1\mathbf{e}+\mathbf{a}_{1}+\mathbf{m}_{1}; all downstream computation (second attention, MLP2, final readout) uses this reduced residual.

Claim 2: 𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{1} is redundant at the final readout.

We keep 𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{1} in the residual for the computation of the second attention and MLP2, but subtract it from the final residual before applying LNf\mathrm{LN}_{f} and the language model head. The readout thus sees 𝐞+𝐚1+𝐚2+𝐦2\mathbf{e}+\mathbf{a}_{1}+\mathbf{a}_{2}+\mathbf{m}_{2} instead of the full five-term sum.

Protocol.

For each of the 40 checkpoints in our grid (sequence lengths ∈{16,32}\in\{16,32\}, vocabulary sizes ∈{128,256,512,1024}\in\{128,256,512,1024\}, 5 seeds), we first classify the model as a two-stage model if per-token accuracy drops below 90% when the second attention is ablated (17 out of 40). For each two-stage model we evaluate both claims on 500 randomly sampled sequences, checking whether the argmax prediction at every sorted-output position agrees with the unmodified forward pass.

Results.

Claim 1 holds universally: across all 17 two-stage models, the argmax agreement is ≥98.5%\geq 98.5\% (mean 99.9%99.9\%). The argmax agreement means the argmax of the logits after removing the redundant circuit remains the same. The direct path of 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} through the residual carries no decision-relevant information beyond what is already encoded in 𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{1}.

Claim 2 holds for 12 of 17 two-stage models (agreement ≥91%\geq 91\%, mean 97.6%97.6\%), but fails for 5 (agreement 22–47%47\%). The failures include the two vocabulary size 10241024 outliers previously identified in Appendix E (sequence length 1616, seed 3 and sequence length 3232, seed 5), where the second attention exploits residual stream components beyond 𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{1}, as well as three additional sequence length 1616 checkpoints (vocabulary size 10241024, seeds 1 and 4; vocabulary size 512512, seed 5). In these models, 𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{1} carries information that is not fully captured by 𝐚2+𝐦2\mathbf{a}_{2}+\mathbf{m}_{2} and is needed at readout.

Figure 29 summarizes both claims across all two-stage models. For the 12 standard two-stage models (excluding the 5 failures), the model’s sorting circuit can be decomposed into a clean pipeline: 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} feeds MLP1 and is then discarded; 𝐦1\mathbf{m}_{1} feeds the second attention and MLP2 and is then discarded; only 𝐞+𝐚2+𝐦2\mathbf{e}+\mathbf{a}_{2}+\mathbf{m}_{2} is needed at readout.

Appendix I Accuracy Without the Second Attention: Dependence on Current Value and Gap

We ablate the second attention (skip it, retain MLP2) and measure per-token accuracy as a function of the current sorted value ii and the gap g=vnext−ig=v_{\mathrm{next}}-i. Figure 30 shows three representative gaps: g=1g=1, g=10g=10, and g=50g=50.

For the smallest gap (g=1g=1), the model without the second attention is nearly at chance when ii is small, but accuracy rises steeply around i≈150i\approx 150 and saturates close to 11 for i≳250i\gtrsim 250. At g=10g=10 a similar ramp appears but saturates at a lower level (≈0.7{\approx}0.7), and at g=50g=50 accuracy remains near zero for all values of ii.

This demonstrates that the first-layer pathway alone can resolve the correct next token only when the target lies close in value to the current token—a regime where the token embedding alone provides enough information without the fine-grained windowed search that the second attention performs. As the gap grows, the second attention becomes indispensable.

Appendix J Corroboration of Gap-Dependent Specialization via Hijacking

This appendix elaborates on the hijacking intervention introduced in the main text (§4.1), which we use to causally corroborate the division of labor across gap sizes. Specifically, for a given input sequence and output position, we independently redirect the direct circuit of the first attention and the attention focus of the second attention toward a different token in the sequence, and measure how often each intervention alone, or both simultaneously, succeeds in steering the model’s prediction to the redirected token.

Figure 4 reports the results, averaged over 23 two-stage seeds on the configuration with sequence length 3232 and vocabulary size 512512, with shaded bands showing ±1\pm 1 standard deviation across seeds. Each panel corresponds to a different minimum gap gg between the current sorted value and the next correct token, and the xx-axis varies the offset of the hijack target (i.e., the redirected token is the one at position i+i+offset in the vocabulary).

When the gap is small (g=1g=1), both the direct-circuit hijack of the first attention (red) and the second attention hijack (blue) individually succeed at rates which vary across seeds. The purple curve shows the fraction of instances in which both interventions independently steer the prediction to the hijacked token on the same input—at gap 11, this co-success rate is approximately 20%20\% on average. This indicates that the final output logit can be shaped by both the direct circuit of the first attention and the output circuit of the second attention simultaneously, akin to a voting mechanism in which the two pathways jointly determine the predicted token.

As the gap increases, the direct circuit of the first attention rapidly loses influence: at g=10g=10 the red curve has already declined substantially, and by g=20g=20 the direct-circuit hijack success rate is near zero. In contrast, the second attention hijack (blue) remains close to 100%100\% across all gap sizes, confirming that for larger gaps the second attention is the dominant, and eventually sole, circuit responsible for specifying the next token. The transition from shared influence at small gaps to second attention dominance at large gaps is consistent with the ablation and attention-mass results described in the main text, providing causal, intervention-based confirmation of gap-dependent specialization.
